query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting Mo with Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will lower the overall electronegativity difference in the lattice, thereby improving dislocation mobility and increasing room‐temperature plasticity without a significant drop in compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, disordered BCC NbZrTiHfMo refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa and relatively low plasticity.
generation.intervention: Replace about 50 atomic percent of Mo with Nb, forming a modified alloy composition such as NbZrTiHf(Mo0.5Nb0.5). This keeps the overall refractory character while reducing the high electronegativity contrast contributed by Mo.
generation.conditions: Prepare both the baseline and modified alloys under the same processing conditions (e.g., arc melting and appropriate homogenization to achieve a disordered BCC structure) and test them via room-temperature compression; control the processing atmosphere, cooling rate, and heat treatment to avoid unwanted secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced overall electronegativity difference in the lattice, leading to fewer dislocation obstacles and a more balanced disordered BCC microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Mo, while contributing to high yield strength, also increases lattice distortions and chemical bonding differences that hinder slip, reducing plasticity. Substituting part of Mo with Nb (which is known to promote ductility in similar refractory HEAs) should mitigate these effects by lessening the electronegativity mismatch, facilitating dislocation motion and enhancing plastic deformation without markedly sacrificing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show an improved balance by exhibiting a higher room-temperature compressive plastic strain while maintaining a compressive yield strength near 1719 MPa.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, which has excellent compressive yield strength (1719 MPa) but suffers from reduced plasticity due to the high Mo content.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect holds if the partial replacement does not trigger secondary phase formation or significantly alter the BCC structure. The exact substitution level (around 50 at.% Mo replaced by Nb) is critical; too little may not yield enough ductility improvement while too much might compromise the strength.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in plastic strain and any minor effect on yield strength will depend on the detailed processing parameters and the final microstructural homogeneity; thus, quantitative changes are uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: the original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo and the modified NbZrTiHf(Mo0.5Nb0.5) using identical processing techniques (e.g., arc melting with homogenization). Carry out room-temperature compression tests and microstructural characterization (XRD, EBSD) for both alloys. Compare compressive yield strength and plastic strain.
measurements: Phase and structure confirmation via XRD/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in compressive plastic strain (without a significant decrease in yield strength compared to ~1719 MPa) relative to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention. In 2010, Senkov and Miracle first published RHEAs, MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW [,]. These two alloys possess body-centered cubic (BCC) structure and have excellent elevated-temperature yield strength which is around 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
